knowledge_type_note: Motif (D), mechanically detectable, defined purely by the value ordering along a line.
definition_short: A line attack where the MORE valuable piece is in front; when it moves, the lesser piece behind it is captured.
definition_long:
The pin's mirror image. A bishop, rook or queen attacks a valuable enemy unit that has a lesser unit directly behind it on the same line. The front piece must move — by force if it is the king — and the piece behind falls.

Skewers are ABSOLUTE when the front piece is the king (the move is compelled) and RELATIVE otherwise (the defender may prefer to lose the exchange, counter-attack, or defend the rear piece).

Skewers are most common in endgames, where kings are exposed on open lines and there are few pieces to interpose.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A friendly line piece attacks an enemy unit with a second enemy unit directly behind it on the same line
The front unit is worth more than the one behind, or is the king
indicators_for: The front unit is the king, so the move is forced
The rear unit is undefended once exposed
indicators_against: The front unit can capture the skewering piece
The front unit can move so that it still defends the rear unit
The rear unit is defended and the exchange is not favourable

exceptions: If the front piece moves along the same line it may keep defending the piece behind.
limitations: Same as the pin: geometry is mechanical, profitability is not.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

examples.note: A clean instance: the detector reports skewer and nothing else, for the move Bxd5+. Two things are verified here and a third is not. VERIFIED: findMotifs() in blind-chess.html reports the motif — and that detector, not this system, is the authority on whether a motif is present. ALSO VERIFIED: Bxd5+ is the recorded solution of a shipped puzzle, and tools/generate_puzzles.js only admits a position when one move is objectively best by a wide margin at confirmation depth, so the move carries engine backing by construction rather than by a separate search here. NOT claimed: that the motif is the whole reason the move wins. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

engine.verdict_note: Inherited validation: this position ships as a puzzle, and the generator's standard is that exactly one move is best by at least GAP_MIN at confirmation depth, re-checked deeper by tools/verify_puzzles.js. The move is therefore engine-verified as best without this base running its own search. The motif label comes from findMotifs, not from the engine — the two are independent and both had to agree for this to be recorded.

examples.note: The skewer proper: the king is in front, must move out of check, and the knight behind it is taken. Paired with the identical men in the other order, which is a pin.

counterexamples.note: The mirror of `pin`'s counterexample and the other half of one controlled pair: the same rook, knight and king on the d-file with the knight in front instead of the king. That is a pin, not a skewer - the piece behind is the more valuable one, which is the whole distinction between the two motifs and the commonest thing a learner gets backwards.

Registered false-positive case `a-skewer-the-front-unit-eats`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Rb1 attacks the black queen on b5 with the rook on b8 directly behind it. More valuable unit in front, less valuable behind, nothing between — the geometry of a skewer, and the detector says so: 'The queen on b5 has to move, and the rook on b8 behind it falls.' WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first indicator_against: "The front unit can capture the skewering piece." The queen is not obliged to move at all; she takes the rook, which is undefended. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Reported at HIGH confidence until a guard was written. Syzygy settles it without an opinion: after Rb1 the position is a WIN FOR BLACK, dtz 1, mate in 7, and the tablebase's own best move is Qxb1+. The guard is one step wider than the record's wording — it asks whether ANY capture of the skewering piece is profitable rather than only the front unit's — and that is deliberate, because a skewering piece somebody else eats is not a skewer either. skewer fell from 11.4% to 7.6% of the 788 shipped puzzles.

tablebase.note: PROVEN, from the mover's side: after Rb1 White is LOST in 7, and the tablebase's best move is Qxb1+. The front unit does not move; it eats.

by_level.beginner: The valuable piece in front has to move, and then you take the piece behind it.
by_level.intermediate: A skewer — the pin turned around, with the bigger piece in front.
by_level.advanced: Skewer, absolute if the front unit is the king. Check whether the front piece can move along the line and keep defending.

beginner_words: the big piece has to move
